about: Who held each office in each term since 1949, the economy during it at every lag from 0 to 4 quarters, and the sources. CC0.

paper.note: The paper charges the first quarter of each term to the previous president (a one-quarter lag), and reports that every other lag from 0 to 4 quarters gives a smaller gap.

notes.text: The 1973 to 1974 oil shock (OPEC I). Blinder and Watson name it as one major reason growth was slower in this term.

source.label: Blinder and Watson, "Presidents and the U.S. Economy: An Econometric Exploration," NBER Working Paper 20324 (2014), published in the American Economic Review 106(4), 2016
source.quote: On balance, growth under Nixon-Ford was markedly slower than under Kennedy-Johnson, and the oil shock of 1973-1974 was one major reason.

notes.text: The 1979 to 1980 oil shock (OPEC II), which Blinder and Watson say helped bring on the high inflation of this term.

source.label: Blinder and Watson, "Presidents and the U.S. Economy: An Econometric Exploration," NBER Working Paper 20324 (2014), published in the American Economic Review 106(4), 2016
source.quote: Carter’s main problem was high inflation—brought on, in part, by OPEC II in 1979-1980.

notes.text: The pandemic of early 2020. NBER dates a recession from February to April 2020, and notes the economy contracted so sharply in March that the first quarter fell well below the last of 2019.

source.label: NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee, announcement of 8 June 2020
source.quote: The economy contracted so sharply in March (the final month of the quarter) that in 2020Q1, GDP, GDI, and employment were significantly below their levels of 2019Q4.
